patient_text: A 55-year-old patient has repeated blood pressure readings around 150/95 mmHg over several visits. There are no acute emergency symptoms.
generated_response:
Probable Diagnosis:
Probable Hypertension. Confirm hypertension using repeated blood pressure measurements rather than a single office reading. In general, use at least three BP measurements per visit across two to three visits at 1-4 week intervals. A diagnosis may be made at a single visit if BP is at least 160/100 mmHg or there is evidence of hypertension-mediated organ damage.

Investigations:
- Perform baseline investigations for hypertension including serum sodium, potassium, creatinine with eGFR, urine dipstick, and 12-lead ECG. If available, obtain lipid profile and fasting glucose. Additional investigations should depend on suspicion of secondary hypertension or hypertension-mediated organ damage.
- Classify dehydration severity before selecting treatment. Severe dehydration is present with one or more danger signs such as lethargy or unconsciousness, absent or weak pulse, or respiratory distress, or with at least two severe dehydration findings such as sunken eyes, inability to drink or drinking poorly, and a skin pinch that returns very slowly. Some dehydration is considered when there are no danger signs and at least two findings such as irritability or restlessness, sunken eyes, rapid pulse, thirst with eager drinking, or a skin pinch that returns slowly. If the patient is awake and alert with normal pulse, normal thirst, eyes not sunken and normal skin pinch, classify as no dehydration.

Medication Planning:
- Use the national primary-care stepwise antihypertensive protocol: start amlodipine 5 mg once daily; if target blood pressure is not reached after review, add losartan 50 mg once daily; if still uncontrolled, add hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg once daily and consider referral when appropriate.

Advice:
- Review monthly after starting or changing antihypertensive treatment until target blood pressure is reached; once controlled, follow up every 3-6 months. Refer to an appropriate specialist when accelerated or malignant hypertension, suspected secondary hypertension, resistant hypertension, recent target-organ damage, pregnancy, or age under 18 years is present.

patient_text: A 40-year-old patient has acute watery diarrhoea, a very weak pulse, sunken eyes and is unable to drink properly. The patient appears severely dehydrated.
generated_response:
Probable Diagnosis:
Probable Cholera. Consider suspected cholera according to outbreak context. Outside a declared cholera outbreak, a patient aged 2 years or older with acute watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration, or dying from acute watery diarrhoea, meets the suspected cholera case definition. During a declared cholera outbreak, any person presenting with or dying from acute watery diarrhoea meets the suspected case definition.

Investigations:
- Classify dehydration severity before selecting treatment. Severe dehydration is present with one or more danger signs such as lethargy or unconsciousness, absent or weak pulse, or respiratory distress, or with at least two severe dehydration findings such as sunken eyes, inability to drink or drinking poorly, and a skin pinch that returns very slowly. Some dehydration is considered when there are no danger signs and at least two findings such as irritability or restlessness, sunken eyes, rapid pulse, thirst with eager drinking, or a skin pinch that returns slowly. If the patient is awake and alert with normal pulse, normal thirst, eyes not sunken and normal skin pinch, classify as no dehydration.

Medication Planning:
- For some dehydration, use Plan B with oral rehydration solution over 4 hours and reassess at least every hour. Give additional ORS to replace ongoing stool losses.
- For patients with no signs of dehydration, use Plan A. Give ORS after each loose stool according to age and continue oral hydration. For patients under 24 months give 50-100 mL after each loose stool; for ages 2-9 years give 100-200 mL; for patients aged 10 years or older give as much as wanted.
- Use antibiotics when the patient has severe dehydration, is pregnant, or is elderly. Preferred treatment is single-dose doxycycline; azithromycin is an alternative. Do not recommend antibiotics solely from this card if these applicability criteria are unknown.

patient_text: A 35-year-old patient presents with acute watery diarrhoea that started today and reports several loose stools.
generated_response:
Probable Diagnosis:
Probable Cholera. Consider suspected cholera according to outbreak context. Outside a declared cholera outbreak, a patient aged 2 years or older with acute watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration, or dying from acute watery diarrhoea, meets the suspected cholera case definition. During a declared cholera outbreak, any person presenting with or dying from acute watery diarrhoea meets the suspected case definition.

Investigations:
- Classify dehydration severity before selecting treatment. Severe dehydration is present with one or more danger signs such as lethargy or unconsciousness, absent or weak pulse, or respiratory distress, or with at least two severe dehydration findings such as sunken eyes, inability to drink or drinking poorly, and a skin pinch that returns very slowly. Some dehydration is considered when there are no danger signs and at least two findings such as irritability or restlessness, sunken eyes, rapid pulse, thirst with eager drinking, or a skin pinch that returns slowly. If the patient is awake and alert with normal pulse, normal thirst, eyes not sunken and normal skin pinch, classify as no dehydration.

Medication Planning:
- For patients with no signs of dehydration, use Plan A. Give ORS after each loose stool according to age and continue oral hydration. For patients under 24 months give 50-100 mL after each loose stool; for ages 2-9 years give 100-200 mL; for patients aged 10 years or older give as much as wanted.
- For some dehydration, use Plan B with oral rehydration solution over 4 hours and reassess at least every hour. Give additional ORS to replace ongoing stool losses.
- Use antibiotics when the patient has severe dehydration, is pregnant, or is elderly. Preferred treatment is single-dose doxycycline; azithromycin is an alternative. Do not recommend antibiotics solely from this card if these applicability criteria are unknown.
